E058-01.notes: Compound predicate 'climbed ... and swept' takes no comma after 'and'; the comma after 'Massachusetts' correctly closes the place appositive. C adds a subject and a stray comma; D's semicolon puts a fragment after it. Facts (Oct 1847, Nantucket rooftop, small telescope) are accurate.

E058-02.notes: A colon after a complete clause introduces the explanatory noun phrase. B (semicolon) and C (period) leave 'a comet that no one had yet reported' as a fragment. D reads 'before a comet' as a preposition phrase, which garbles the meaning. 'Near the North Star' and 'no one had yet reported' are accurate: de Vico found it independently a few days later.

E058-03.notes: The participial phrase must modify Mitchell. A modifies the medal, B modifies Mitchell's medal, and D modifies the medal; all three dangle. The medal facts check out: Christian VIII's standing offer for telescopic comets, awarded in 1848. Saying 'King of Denmark' without naming him is fine.

flags.note: 'her list of honors' is slightly loose. The list is the writer's account of Mitchell's honors, not a list Mitchell made; 'the list of Mitchell's honors' would be cleaner. Also, A-C are so plainly wrong (C even misstates the sentence, which does not contradict Massachusetts) that D is easy to pick by elimination.

E058-04.notes: The geographic aside is irrelevant to a paragraph about her honors. Nantucket really is about 30 miles south of Cape Cod.

E058-05.notes: 'where' correctly refers back to the place, Vassar College. B 'which she taught astronomy' leaves no role for 'which'. C 'when' points illogically to 1865 for a twenty-year span. D 'in that' changes the meaning to a cause. Facts: Vassar opened in 1865 and Mitchell taught there until 1888, so 'more than twenty years' is correct.

E058-06.notes: Parallelism: 'by observing ... rather than reading'. A mixes a gerund with an infinitive. C puts a clause after 'rather than' and breaks the 'by ___' structure. D's perfect participle is illogical here.

E058-07.notes: Simple past 'led' fits 'In 1878'. 'lead' is a common misspelling trap, 'leaded' is not a form of the verb, and 'has led' clashes with a fixed past date. The 1878 total eclipse and Denver trip with students are accurate (July 29, 1878).

E058-08.notes: Sentence 9 gives an example of the general claim 'fought for fair treatment'. There is no contrast for However or Instead, and no cause-effect for As a result. The raise episode (younger male professors paid more; she protested and got a raise) matches standard accounts.

E058-09.notes: The interrupter needs matching punctuation on both sides. A and B mix a dash with a comma. C's single dash was the strongest rival case, as an end-of-sentence emphatic dash, but it leaves 'demanded' cut off from its shared object 'a raise', so it reads as an unclosed interruption. Paired dashes in D are the only clean option. The C trap may draw a fair number of test takers.

E058-10.notes: The essay is a biographical sketch, not an explanation of comet-finding methods. A overstates a single descriptive detail. C misstates the passage, which says nothing about why the offer existed. D is factually false about the passage.

E058-11.notes: Concision: A, B and D each repeat the same idea (carefully/meticulously, closely/with care, closely/in a careful way). C is the only option that is not redundant and keeps the meaning. Lee facts are accurate: Harvard seminars, Nutshell Studies, 1 in. = 1 ft scale, Baltimore OCME, most of the original 20 survive. The other errors in the passage belong to other items.
